articles.title: 'Misleading': Election Commission rejects claims of vote-count discrepancies in 2024 polls
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Wednesday rejected social media claims of discrepancies between the number of votes polled and votes
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Wednesday rejected social media claims of discrepancies between the number of votes polled and votes counted in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and state assembly polls describing the allegations as "misleading."In a post on X, the poll body shared screenshots of claims concerning constituencies in Maharashtra, Haryana and Jammu and Kashmir, along with constituency-wise data to clarify the figures."This is with reference to a social media post claiming inconsistencies in the number of votes polled and votes counted in the General Elections to the Lok Sabha, 2024 and General Elections to Legislative Assemblies of States held in 2024," the ECI said in a statement.The Commission said it publishes details of electors, votes polled through electronic voting machines (EVMs), postal ballots and total votes cast in its statistical reports and index cards. These records are available on its website.It also questioned the reference to "internal records" in the claims, saying the post had named certain constituencies and alleged that the ECI had counted zero votes there, but had not specified which records it was relying on.The Commission said Form 17C is the sole statutory account of votes cast at a polling station. It is prepared by the presiding officer at the close of polling.Copies of Part-I of Form 17C are given to polling agents appointed by candidates who are present at the polling station when voting concludes, the ECI said.On counting day, candidates' counting agents match the number of votes polled, recorded in Part-I of Form 17C, with the total number of votes counted, recorded in Part-II of the form.The Commission reiterated that all election-related data, including the number of votes polled and counted, had been made available through its statistical reports and index cards.It said the claims of discrepancies in the constituencies cited in the report were misleading and shared constituency-wise details to clarify the figures.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Russia, Ukraine agree to large prisoner swap after Abu Dhabi talks
articles.summary: Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a “large-scale” exchange of prisoners of war, following two days of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi. Negotiators are traveling back to their capitals to finalize details, Rustem Umerov, the head of the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, said in a post on the social platform X. “There are opportunities…
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a “large-scale” exchange of prisoners of war, following two days of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi.

Negotiators are traveling back to their capitals to finalize details, Rustem Umerov, the head of the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, said in a post on the social platform X.

“There are opportunities to continue the negotiation process,” Umerov said, but he cautioned significant differences remain and that there is “a great deal of difficult work ahead”.

The prisoner swap was also confirmed by the head of the Russian negotiating delegation, Vladimir Medinsky. He told Russian state TV that the future security architecture of Europe was a central point in the talks.

The U.S. team was led by President Trump’s top envoys for peace missions: Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, and business partner and close friend Steve Witkoff. The talks marked the first negotiations between Russia and Ukraine in nine months.

Kushner and Witkoff are headed to Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin to go over the topics discussed in Abu Dhabi and will then travel to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Kushner said one of the goals of the Moscow meetings is to “try and see if” Europeans can be added to the negotiation format. Kushner said he and Witkoff convened with representatives from the European Union, NATO, the United Kingdom, Italy, Germany and France ahead of the Ukraine-Russia talks.

Kushner described the Russia-Ukraine talks as “substantive” and “tough.”

“Some areas we see places where we can find compromises, others we need to have more discussions, but I think this was a good first step,” he said.

Kushner and Witkoff are pushing for a deal between Russia and Ukraine that would lay out the postwar scenario for both sides, security guarantees for Ukraine and a security architecture in Europe that they say would take into account Russia’s concerns. Confidence in postwar security would allow for decisions on Ukrainian territorial concessions, they argue.

“We also discussed the hard issues … the territorial issues, which will be the hardest. But we do believe that as we discuss these other issues, we’ll find a pathway to settle them all at the same time,” Kushner said at a press conference following the conclusion of talks.

Skeptics of Moscow’s demands say the discussions surrounding security architecture in Europe are part of a Russian talking point to justify their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, blaming NATO’s westward expansion as a provocation.

“We have a European security architecture in place. I’ve counted at least 30 international agreements where Russia has undertaken obligations, to respect sovereignty and territorial integrity … our problem is, is that Russia is not keeping to those agreements,” Kaja Kallas, the top foreign policy official for the European Union, said on Monday following a Group of Seven foreign ministers meeting.

“The only one that is breaching that security architecture is Russia. That’s why we have to make sure that in those talks there are clear concessions from the Russian side, otherwise we’ll just see more of these attacks.”

articles.title: In 1994, Jane Seymour bought a $3.4 million Malibu home; after at least six wildfire scares and a narrow escape in 2024, she says she will not sell and has replaced flammable plants to protect her oceanfront property
articles.summary: Some homeowners may decide that several encounters with natural disasters are enough and move somewhere safer.
articles.body: Some homeowners may decide that several encounters with natural disasters are enough and move somewhere safer. But for actress Jane Seymour the answer is to stay, adapt and protect the place she has called home for more than three decades. The actress has been evacuated numerous times from wildfires and had a scary close call in December 2024, but she has no plans to leave her Malibu oceanfront estate; instead, she is opting to fortify it against the possibility of another fire.Seymour, 75, remains very attached to the California coastal community, where she has made her home since buying the property in 1994 for $3.4 million, Page Six reports.A Malibu home worth keepingSeymour’s 6,326 square-foot oceanfront property has been her sanctuary for more than 30 years. The former Bond girl, who was born in Middlesex, England, has been all over the world in her career, but still believes Malibu is a particularly special spot, Page Six reports.The report further states that she is tied to the neighborhood in ways that go beyond the property. The actress loves the tight-knit community and has said she plans to continue her support as the area is under the threat of repeated wildfires.Seymour herself has experienced at least six fires in Malibu, Page Six reports, and the one in December 2024 brought the danger uncomfortably close to home. Her house was almost destroyed, highlighting the need for caution in an area where the natural environment and powerful Santa Ana winds can combine to create hazardous situations.But the actress is determined to stay, believing that living close to nature also means learning to respect its unpredictability.Alter garden to reduce fire hazardsRather than thinking about moving, Seymour has turned her attention to making her surroundings safer. One of her most consequential preventive actions was completely rethinking the landscaping around her home, states Bang Showbiz.The report also states that she cleared out plants that weren’t drought-tolerant or prone to catching fire, replacing them with vegetation better suited to the region’s arid climate. She made the changes after consulting local fire officials who told her what she needed to do to make the property less vulnerable.Seymour took the recommendations seriously, doing everything in her power to protect her home, Page Six and Bang Showbiz report. But she also knows preparation can’t eliminate all hazards, especially when wildfires are unpredictable.She has other fire-fighting measures on her property as well. These include fire hydrants and a system that allows water to be drawn from the swimming pool, providing additional resources in an emergency.60 years of nature's unpredictabilityThe challenges Seymour faced are typical of California's fire-prone coastal communities. Wildfire preparedness is ongoing in Malibu due to its dry vegetation and strong seasonal winds.The actress gives the local fire department special thanks for protecting her property and neighborhood for years.It describes how homeowners can reduce hazards by choosing fire-resistant landscaping and installing emergency water systems.A new chapter beyond Hollywood Away from her Malibu estate, Seymour continues to pursue creative projects. Her latest venture includes a lab-grown diamond jewellery collection developed in collaboration with QVC's Soul to Soul line, launched on November 6.The collection features sterling silver earrings, pendant necklaces, rings and bangles. For Seymour, the designs reflect personal experiences, relationships, and important connections, giving them emotional value beyond their material value.Her personal life is also changing for the better. The actress confirmed her engagement to musician and physician John Zambetti in June. Interestingly, the proposal took place at her Malibu residence, although the romantic moment did not unfold entirely as planned.As reported by Bang Showbiz, Zambetti struggled to retrieve the engagement ring after it accidentally slipped onto the bed, leaving him temporarily stuck underneath it. In the end the couple ended up laughing about the rather unconventional proposal.For Seymour, the Malibu home is still much more than just an expensive oceanfront address. It is where she has created memories, relationships and celebrated some of life’s biggest milestones. Despite repeated wildfire scares she is determined to protect the property and the community around it, proving that sometimes the strongest attachment to a home is measured not by its value but by the determination to preserve it.Images Courtesy: Instagram/Jane Seymour and istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: WTO rules should be a foundation for new trade policy
articles.summary: It offers the most effective baseline for U.S. economic relations with much of the world, regardless of the need to depart from or supplement it.
articles.body:
As demonstrated in last week’s election, Americans are tired of trade wars and tariff chaos.

The response to chaos is rules — rules that provide the stability and predictability businesses need to operate. Rules that allow consumers to know that the prices paid today will not double tomorrow because of arbitrary tariffs, and that assure the U.S. trading partners of today that they will not be adversaries tomorrow based on the arbitrary whims of one man.

Polls suggest that much of the U.S. public agrees. A recent Council on Foreign Relations poll found that 49 percent of Americans believe that fair trade means that all countries are bound by the same rules.

But where to find these rules? There is no need to reinvent the wheel, and certainly no easy way to do so. The World Trade Organization rulebook is extensive, and (even now) widely followed. It is also largely the product of U.S. economic priorities. Whatever the organization’s flaws and limitations, for now, it offers the most effective baseline for U.S. economic relations with much of the world, regardless of the need to depart from or supplement it.

The WTO rulebook is comprehensive, covering limitations on discriminatory treatment of imported goods and commitments to limit and remedy injurious subsidization. It also ensures transparent regulatory processes and efficient customs procedures and protects market access for the trade of services, among other topics.

These rules are not the arbitrary product of a faceless bureaucracy. Every element in the World Trade Organization rulebook was negotiated by member countries and agreed by full consensus. They embody economic cooperation and stable economic relations. Compliance does not represent swearing fealty to abstract principles. Rather, it is a means of avoiding real world economic harm to other nations (and your own nation) and limiting frictions that undermine cooperation on projects both within and beyond the trade sphere.

Much attention is correctly paid to the the World Trade Organization’s inability to address modern challenges such as Chinese overcapacity, supply chain resilience and a fragmenting geopolitical landscape marked by aggressive territorial claims and outright invasions. But that inability does not diminish the value of the rules that do exist.

Some 70 percent of world trade continues to take place under World Trade Organization rules, underscoring the value countries continue to see in compliance with the rules. And as I noted in testimony before the House Committee on Ways and Means Trade Subcommittee earlier this year, a less obstructionist approach by a handful of members would unlock progress on several agreements that would at least partially restore the organization’s relevance as a negotiating forum.

Apart from the existing rulebook and the still operational monitoring function, an effective WTO dispute settlement system would play an important role in preventing escalating trade wars. Losing parties are more willing to accept outcomes of a process they view as fair, and under WTO rules, retaliation for non-compliance is limited to the impact of the offending measure.

However, the U.S. broke the system in 2019 over concerns about judicial overreach in the organization’s appellate body. While restoring the system by addressing these concerns would be valuable, compliance with existing rules largely continues today because of members’ mutual interest in stable trade relationships.

Given the difficulty of developing new rules, other arrangements may be necessary. But that does not diminish the value of the World Trade Organization’s rules as a baseline of global economic cooperation, particularly because any other arrangements would not likely have the same breadth of membership or issues covered.

Any efforts to make such new arrangements will need to contend with two questions — how to get there, and what to do in the meantime. A U.S. recommitment to the World Trade Organization will be essential to answering both questions. Any supplemental or alternative arrangements will take time to negotiate. For now, we must reaffirm the existing rules-based order to stem the chaos of retreat from those rules by the U.S. and others in response.

No arrangements will be easily reached without restoring trust in the U.S. as a reliable negotiating partner. That trust is now at a low ebb, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s statements have illustrate d . Rebuilding confidence will require the restoration of U.S. tariff policies that distinguish between friends and adversaries and rein-in presidential tariff authorities. It will also require the U.S. to demonstrate that it is committed to rules, while also acknowledging that they are a baseline from which it may be necessary to depart.

This will require the U.S. to clearly articulate the criteria by which it intends to depart from the rules. That could include rules based on whether a country’s products benefit from non-market policies and subsidization geared toward dominating a particular sector, perhaps with the additional requirement that the country has a track record of weaponizing that dominance.

Such clarity would highlighting deficiencies in the current rules and show our trading partners that any departures from the rules will be predictable and subject to limits — and not directed at them. And since those partners are gaining a more concrete understanding of why the world must urgently address China’s trade measures, those assurances could be critical to developing an effective international response .

Bruce Hirsh is principal at Tailwind Global Strategies. He previously served in senior positions at the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative and the Senate Finance Committee.

articles.title: Russian ambassador to US dies suddenly, foreign ministry says
articles.summary: Russia’s ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, has died aged 66, the Russian Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday. It did not mention the cause of his death.
articles.body: Russia’s ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, has died aged 66, the Russian Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday. It did not mention the cause of his death. Darchiev “passed away suddenly,” the ministry said in a statement, describing him as an “exceptional professional.” “Alexander Darchiev served in one of the most demanding areas of Russian foreign policy,” the statement said. “We extend our deepest and most heartfelt condolences to Alexander Darchiev’s family and loved ones.” Darchiev, a veteran diplomat known for his stinging condemnations of the West, had served as ambassador to Washington since March 2025. His time in office was marked by a thawing of US-Russia relations as President Donald Trump opened bilateral talks with Moscow and scaled back aid to Ukraine. Darchiev previously headed the Russian Foreign Ministry’s North Atlantic Department in Washington, according to the Russian embassy in the US, as well as serving as Russia’s ambassador to Canada from 2014 to 2021. Nearly a decade ago another Russian diplomat died suddenly aged 64. Vitaly Churkin, an ambassador to the UN, passed away following cardiac arrest in 2017, just one day before his 65th birthday. The average life expectancy for a man in Russia is 68 years old, according to the World Bank. This is a developing story and will be updated.

That photo of the property, which Bessent reportedly purchased for $12.5 million, allowed individuals to geo-locate the Treasury secretary’s home, the source noted.

Other administration officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, are living on military bases.

The Iran conflict , which began in late February, has stretched on despite President Trump initially saying it would last roughly one month.

Americans’ frustrations with high gas prices amid the war gave Democrats a political opening, which they capitalized on via last week’s sweeping midterm victories .

Trump said Tuesday the U.S. military was maintaining its naval blockade of Iranian ports. But the president claimed the war was “ending quickly,” adding his administration is trying “to take care of people that have been very good to us over the years” in the Middle East.

articles.title: Stephen Miller’s White House will test Mexico’s red lines
articles.summary: Mexico’s security chief, Omar García Harfuch, should already be preparing for a White House that acts alone, possibly in opposition to Congress.
articles.body:
On Friday, President Trump named Stephen Miller , the architect of his immigration agenda, as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles three days after Democrats won both chambers of Congress. As many of us who have watched him evolve since the first Trump administration, this appointment matters more for Mexico than the midterm results.

Although Miller’s fixation on immigration has fallen out of favor with voters, that will not stop him from coercing Mexico on security, with more open threats of direct U.S. military action. Mexico’s security chief, Omar Garcia Harfuch, should already be preparing for a White House that acts alone, possibly in opposition to Congress.

Miller has not been shy about how he sees the problem. At the Pentagon’s counter-cartel conference in Miami this past March, he called the cartels “the ISIS and al Qaeda of this hemisphere” and said they should be met with hard power and lethal force rather than criminal justice.

That describes a policy already in place: eight Mexican criminal groups designated foreign terrorist organizations since February 2025, ongoing lethal strikes on suspected drug boats since September 2025, and around 500 troops sent to the Texas border this fall after an alleged shooting. As deputy chief of staff, Miller helped shape these decisions. As chief of staff, he controls who reaches the president and what lands on his desk. The officials who counseled patience with Mexico, if any remain, now have fewer ways in.

A Democratic Congress and the Republicans losses of so many elected positions across border states will not change this. If anything, Miller will push the White House toward the tools it controls alone: terrorist designations, Treasury sanctions, indictments, troop deployments and covert actions.

Unless Congress stops him, Miller will encourage Trump to continue using the cudgel of tariffs to exact concessions from President Claudia Sheinbaum. All of these are exactly the tools that reach into Mexico and weaken her presidency.

For two years, Mexico has answered relentless pressure with results. President Sheinbaum has granted unimaginable concessions to avoid direct attack on Mexico’s sovereignty.

Under her administration, Mexico has extradited or transferred 133 cartel figures to the United States in 2025 and 37 more in January. In February, a raid built on U.S.-shared intelligence killed Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as “El Mencho,” leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel. Up to now, President Claudia Sheinbaum has run a two-track strategy of sovereignty rhetoric in her morning press conferences but close cooperation in practice.

Nevertheless, that cooperation has bought Mexico time, not safety. Eduardo Guerrero, one of Mexico’s sharpest security analysts, has tracked this dynamic all year. In January, he called each batch of transferred prisoners an offering to Uncle Sam and predicted that the National Palace will end up yielding once again to Washington. He judged a ground invasion unlikely, but said rapid drone strikes on cartel or political targets are possible.

In July, he described Washington’s turn from a war on drugs to a war on cartels : State, Justice, Treasury, the FBI and Homeland Security now treat cartel finances, logistics, and political protectors as terrorist infrastructure. In other words, the legal and bureaucratic architecture for unilateral action already exists. This is the landscape Miller inherits, with no guardrails on how he will use it.

The targets are also changing. In April, U.S. prosecutors charged Sinaloa Governor Ruben Rocha Moya, a member of Sheinbaum’s Morena party, along with nine officials. Mexico refused to extradite them, despite their possible links to organized crime. The same month, two CIA officers died in a crash in Chihuahua after a joint operation the federal government says it never authorized. Mexico’s attorney general has since charged a former Chihuahua prosecutor with treason for allowing U.S. involvement in the operation.

Guerrero asks the right question : Why is cooperation with Washington indispensable when the federal government runs it, and treason when a state does? The answer, I think, is that Mexico City already expects Washington to go around its authority and is trying to close every side door.

That is why García Harfuch must plan for unilateral action rather than for another round of intelligence sharing. He knows better than most how Mexico’s security apparatus behaves under foreign pressure: His father led the Federal Security Directorate in the late 1970s. Planning means protocols for what Mexico does if a U.S. strike lands on its territory. It means a public line on sovereignty settled before a crisis and protecting the state officials that cooperate in good faith.

It also means telling Washington plainly what decapitation has produced. Felipe Calderón’s kingpin strategy from 2006-2012 splintered the cartels, multiplied the violence and expanded the reach of organized crime. The removal of Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzman and Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada set off a brutal war between factions of the Sinaloa Cartel that continues today. Targeting leaders satisfies Washington, but it has fueled a crisis of insecurity and weakened the rule of law.

Coercion from Washington has produced cooperation from Mexico. The cost of that cooperation has fallen on migrants, border communities and Mexico’s weakest institutions and most vulnerable populations. Under Miller, that cost will grow.

Gladys McCormick is the Jay and Debe Moskowitz Endowed Chair in Mexico-U.S. relations at the Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs at Syracuse University. She has previously served as a senior associate at the Center for International and Strategic Studies in Washington.

articles.title: The SS United States broke the transatlantic speed record in 1952 and spent 29 years docked in Philadelphia; the 990-foot liner is set to be sunk off Florida on November 11 to become the world's largest artificial reef
articles.summary: For a ship once celebrated as a symbol of American engineering and maritime ambition, the SS United States is preparing for an extraordinary final chapter
articles.body: For a ship once celebrated as a symbol of American engineering and maritime ambition, the SS United States is preparing for an extraordinary final chapter beneath the waves. After carrying generations of passengers across the Atlantic and spending decades tied to Philadelphia's waterfront, the legendary ocean liner is being transformed into an underwater attraction. Its planned deployment off Florida has now been brought forward by a day, with officials citing changing weather conditions as the reason for the revised schedule.A historic farewell moves forwardThe 990-foot vessel is scheduled to be sunk on Wednesday, November 11, rather than Thursday, as originally planned. According to CBS News, Okaloosa County officials announced the change on Monday night, explaining that forecasts indicated more favourable conditions for the operation earlier in the week.The deployment is expected to begin at 1 p.m. Central Standard Time in the Gulf of Mexico, approximately 22 nautical miles southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach. The date also coincides with Veterans Day, giving the operation an additional symbolic significance for a ship that carries the name of the United States.Advance Local reported that Wednesday's forecast called for winds of five to 10 knots and seas of one foot or less. Conditions were expected to deteriorate on Thursday, with winds potentially reaching 15 to 20 knots, gusts of up to 25 knots and waves measuring two to three feet. Forecasts farther west also indicated rougher seas.From transatlantic record-holder to underwater landmarkThe SS United States entered maritime history with its maiden voyage in 1952. During its crossing from New York to Europe, the ocean liner established a transatlantic speed record, completing the journey in just three days. More than seven decades later, it continues to hold the record for the fastest west-to-east crossing by an ocean liner.As 6ABC News reported, the vessel is regarded as a significant example of American maritime engineering. Its passengers included presidents, film stars and ordinary travellers, while one of its most unusual cargoes was the Mona Lisa.The ship was also designated for the National Register of Historic Places in 1999, recognising its place in the country's maritime heritage. However, after its years of service, it spent nearly three decades docked along Philadelphia's Delaware River waterfront, becoming a familiar sight in South Philadelphia.Preparations for its final deploymentThe liner's transformation into an artificial reef has involved extensive preparation. After leaving Philadelphia last year, it was towed to Mobile, Alabama, where remediation work began in March 2025.Advance Local reported that crews spent approximately a year and a half preparing the hull, removing loose paint and hazardous materials before it could be deployed underwater. The vessel's distinctive funnels and several other artefacts were also removed and preserved, allowing important elements of its appearance to survive beyond the sinking.The ship was subsequently towed out of Mobile early Monday for its final journey towards Florida.A new attraction beneath the GulfOkaloosa County acquired the vessel's hull with the intention of creating an artificial reef that could attract recreational divers and anglers while providing a habitat for marine life. Officials have also presented the project as an opportunity to support tourism and local economic development.According to 6ABC News, the county hopes the massive structure will attract divers and improve the underwater ecosystem.The operation will require careful coordination because hundreds of vessels could potentially gather to watch the deployment. Advance Local reported that the US Coast Guard will enforce a one-nautical-mile exclusion zone around the site. Boats entering the restricted area without authorisation could face boarding, civil penalties or further enforcement action.A livestream is expected to allow viewers to follow the historic event, with coverage scheduled ahead of the deployment. A planned send-off ceremony has been cancelled, while a viewing gathering is expected at AJ's Seafood and Oyster Bar in Destin.From setting an enduring speed record to becoming one of the largest artificial reefs ever created, the SS United States is poised to exchange its place in maritime history for a new life beneath the Gulf of Mexico.Image Courtesy: Advance LocalYou use AI every day. articles.title: Implications of Poland’s constitutional crisis
articles.summary: Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s recent actions to restore the rule of law by replacing Constitutional Tribunal judges and implementing strict censorship laws have ignited a constitutional crisis between the Polish government and President Karol Nawrocki.
articles.body:
Poland’s constitutional crisis started on Oct. 30 when the riot police brought from all over the country entered the building of the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw. The building was quiet, as most people had left to visit family graves for All Saints Day and the Polish president was on a diplomatic mission to Senegal.

Then it was announced that the tribunal’s president and his deputy were suspended, barred from their offices and replaced by judges appointed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who entered the building through a back door from his office.

President Karol Nawrocki turned his plane around and returned to enter the Tribunal at the request of legitimate judges through layers of masked riot police armed with machine guns. His presence did not resolve the crisis. He left calling for all political forces to compromise and requested consultations with other judges and political leaders. But Tusk announced that he is restoring “rule of law” and that there is no compromise .

This conflict started in 2015 , when the outgoing government of Tusk’s party appointed five judges to the Constitutional Tribunal instead of three. The other two were supposed to be appointed by the newly elected conservative Parliament. Their subsequent replacement sparked accusations by European institutions of the violation of the rule of law. Currently, the European Commission fully supports Tusk’s actions.

In this crisis, both sides claim they are right and acting in a legal manner. What is significant is that Tusk is using arguments based on the European Union laws and directives, while Nawrocki says he is protecting the Polish Constitution and laws.

The Constitutional Tribunal issued a decision in 2021 establishing that Polish law takes precedence over European law , similar to what was decided by Germany’s constitutional court. Thus, the law that is valid right now is the Polish constitution, but Tusk and his European backers do not accept it. They claim that the rule of law prevails only when the European Union laws are applied under jurisdiction of European courts. These courts constantly expand sovereign areas of authority to the European Commission. Thus, the demand is for the political authority to be transferred outside of Poland to a centralized institution lacking any democratic legitimacy or supervision.

And so for this constitutional takeover to actually become quasi-legal, new judges appointed by Tusk who do not meet constitutional requirements will have to reverse the previous rulings Poland’s legal sovereignty. To prevent criticism of such moves, another crucial priority is a law that muzzles free speech on the internet and social media.

Such a law was adopted on Nov. 6. In the first part, it adopts the EU Directive called “Democracy Shield,” which fights disinformation, upholds European values and rule of law and prevents foreign interference in elections. It imposes sanctions upon those who violate it.

The second part is an additional radical layer of punishments championed by the current government. For vague violations, such as threats to national security or public order, hate speech or Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference, the government imposes draconian punishments such as seizures of property of individuals, corporations and non-governmental organizations to be immediately auctioned off, up to $5 million in fines, up to 12 years in prison, or to be put on a permanent sanctions list with a loss of political and economic rights.

These punishments are to be decided by a single government official with no right of appeal. The originator of this law is Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski and his office will be in charge of its implementation.

The Polish law is far more radical than the EU law. It targets not only offending individuals but also their families and friends. Its purpose is to control independent voices outside of mainstream media.

This has serious implications for the conduct of European elections. In addition to funding activist non-governmental organizations and withholding EU funds, the government and the EU will control the whole information environment with heavy sanctions for arbitrarily defined “disinformation.”

Perhaps the example of this misuse was demonstrated by the interior minister this weekend when he characterized the man suspected of perpetrating a mass attack in Poland as having “far-right extremist views.” There are no indications so far that he held such views. Local investigators report that the man was quiet, always dressed in black with a hood on his head and black painted nails, a good student and critical of the Catholic Church. It seems that the “far-right” label was only indicated to tar his conservative political opponents with terrorism associations.

The EU takeover of the Constitutional Tribunal used violence to establish what is really an illegitimate rule of law. The censorship law muzzles independent voices criticizing the government and the European Union, giving primacy to undemocratic, centralized, international bureaucratic institutions. Poland and Europe will pay dearly for it.

Lucja Swiatkowski Cannon, Ph.D., is a Research Professor at the Institute of World Politics in Washington.
